Indus Valley Civilization.sub: Explore Harappan cities, homes, jobs and trade through simple examples.

s.h: Start here: who were the Harappans?
p: Picture a busy town with brick homes, wells and drains. People grow food, make pots and trade goods. This is a useful way to think about Harappan life. We also call it the Indus Valley Civilisation.

Its main urban phase was about 2600–1900 BCE. Urban means linked with towns and cities. BCE means Before Common Era. With BCE dates, the larger number comes first. The dates are rough guides, not exact start and end dates.
Sites lie in parts of present-day India and Pakistan. Harappa gave the civilisation its name. It was a Bronze Age culture. People used copper and bronze, as well as stone tools.

s.h: How do we learn about them?
p: We learn from things left in the ground. These include homes, pots, tools, bones and seals. An archaeologist studies such remains to learn about the past. A seal is a small object used to make a mark.

Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa in 1921. R. D. Banerji worked at Mohenjo-daro in 1922. In 1924, John Marshall announced the civilisation to the wider world. These are modern discovery dates. They are not the dates when the cities were built.

The Indus script is still unread. Script means a system of written signs. Think of a puzzle with missing pieces. We have many clues, but cannot yet read the signs with confidence. So we must be careful about claims naming kings or gods.

Many Harappan cities had planned streets and brick buildings. Some homes had bathing spaces. Water flowed into drains. Many bricks followed standard sizes. The plans differed from one site to another.

Here is a simple example. If every family pours dirty water into the street, everyone suffers. Shared drains work better, but people must build and maintain them together. This helps show why planning mattered.
Mohenjo-daro is known for the Great Bath. It was built with care to hold water. Its exact use is still debated. Do not assume Harappan drains worked like modern sewage treatment plants.
People grew crops such as wheat and barley. They kept animals too. Some made pottery, beads and metal tools. Cotton was known. Different kinds of work helped support city life.

Imagine a farmer, a potter and a bead maker. The farmer has grain. The potter has jars. The bead maker has ornaments. Trade lets them exchange what they make. Standard weights helped measure goods in a more consistent way.

The Harappans had trade links with Mesopotamia. Texts there mention Meluhha, often linked with the Harappan region. This does not mean every person travelled abroad. Nor does it mean they used modern coins.

s.h: Match each site with a clue
p: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are in present-day Pakistan. Match Mohenjo-daro with the Great Bath. Dholavira in Gujarat is known for reservoirs. A reservoir stores water for later use.
Kalibangan in Rajasthan has evidence of a ploughed field. Lothal in Gujarat is linked with bead work. It also has a basin often called a dockyard. Scholars still debate that use.
Memory tip: picture Dholavira storing water during dry times. Connecting a name with a useful feature is easier than learning a list alone. But one feature cannot tell the whole story of a city.

s.h: Why did the large cities decline?
p: Around 1900 BCE, large urban centres began to weaken. People still lived in many places. The end of a city system does not mean all its people vanished.
River changes, climate pressures and shifts in trade may have played a part. Different regions may have faced different problems. There is no single proven cause for every city.

Imagine a town whose river route becomes hard to use. Farms, travel and trade may all suffer. This example shows how several pressures can work together. It is not proof that one event destroyed every Harappan city.

Remember this sequence: farms and settlements → large cities → crafts and trade → changes in urban life. Connect each feature with its purpose. Drains helped manage dirty water. Weights helped measure goods.
Common traps: the script is still unread. The Harappans belonged to the Bronze Age. The modern discovery of Harappa was not the start of the civilisation. Dates such as 2600 BCE are approximate.
Try this: why do standard weights matter in a market? They help buyers and sellers measure goods on a shared basis. That is a clearer answer than just listing the word weights.

sum: Main urban phase: about 2600–1900 BCE.
The script is still unread, so some questions remain open.
Planning, farming, crafts and trade supported city life.
Urban decline had several possible causes; settlement continued.

Mauryan and Gupta Empires.sub: Keep the two empires clear with short explanations, examples and memory tips.

p: The Mauryas and Guptas were different ruling families. A ruling family is also called a dynasty. Several centuries separate these two dynasties.

Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire around 322 BCE. Bindusara and Ashoka were later Mauryan rulers. Gupta power grew in the fourth century CE. Major Gupta rulers included Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II.

Think of two pupils with the same first name. They are still different people. In the same way, Chandragupta Maurya and Chandragupta I were not one ruler. Always add the dynasty or number to the name.

s.h: How did the Mauryas run an empire?
p: An empire rules a large area with many communities. It needs more than a strong army. It also needs officials, income, roads and messages. Pataliputra, near modern Patna, was an important political centre.

Imagine running shops in several towns. You need trusted staff and clear accounts. News must reach each branch. This helps explain some problems rulers faced. It is only a comparison, not an exact map of Mauryan rule.

Chanakya, also called Kautilya, is traditionally linked with Chandragupta Maurya. The Arthashastra is traditionally linked with Kautilya. Scholars debate when its different parts were composed. Megasthenes wrote Indica about India. We know much of it through later writers.
Ashoka conquered Kalinga around 261 BCE. His own messages describe the suffering caused by the war. These messages were carved on rocks and pillars. Such carved writing is called an inscription.
After the war, Ashoka stressed dhamma. This included good conduct, care for people and respect for different faiths. It was not simply an order for everyone to follow one religion.

Think of neighbours with different beliefs. They can still agree to treat each other with respect. That helps explain the public message of dhamma. Ashoka supported Buddhism, but his wider message reached people from many groups.
Ashoka's inscriptions survive from his own reign. A reign is the time a ruler is in power. Many use Prakrit and the Brahmi script. Some regions used other languages and scripts.
Rock Edict XIII is a key source for Kalinga and its aftermath. Edict means a public order or message from a ruler. A message carved in several places could reach people far from the capital.
But a ruler's message is not proof that everyone followed it. Think of a public notice. It tells you the rule, but not how every person acted. Historians compare several kinds of evidence.

Chandragupta I helped strengthen Gupta power. Samudragupta led many campaigns. Harishena praised him in the Prayaga pillar inscription. Prayaga is also linked with the name Allahabad in older references.
Chandragupta II is linked with further growth of the empire. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian visited India in this broad period. A pilgrim travels for religious reasons.
Some areas were ruled directly. In other areas, local rulers accepted Gupta authority and paid tribute. Tribute is a payment made to a stronger ruler. So control was not the same in every place.

s.h: Books, art, science and the golden age label
p: The Gupta period saw notable work in literature, art, maths and astronomy. Astronomy is the study of objects in the sky. Kalidasa is linked with Sanskrit literature. Aryabhata's work belongs to this broad era.
Some books call this a golden age. The phrase points to great achievements. It does not mean all people were wealthy or had equal rights.

Think of a town with fine buildings and famous writers. Some people there may still be poor. This example helps separate cultural success from the wellbeing of every person. Do not give one ruler or thinker credit for all ancient learning.

Large empires can weaken for several reasons. These include wars, disputes over the throne and a lack of resources. Local rulers may also gain power. The Mauryan system broke up after Ashoka's time. Gupta power later faced several pressures, including invasions.
For the Mauryas, remember Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka and dhamma. For the Guptas, remember Samudragupta, Harishena and major cultural works. Keeping the two groups apart prevents many exam errors.
Try this question: what is special about an inscription from a ruler's own time? It gives evidence from that period. But we must still check its purpose and claims.

sum: The Mauryas and Guptas were different dynasties.
Ashoka's inscriptions explain his public message of dhamma.
Harishena's inscription praises Samudragupta.
A golden age for culture does not mean equal wealth for all.

Delhi Sultanate.sub: Learn the five dynasties and key terms through short, clear examples.

p: The Delhi Sultanate lasted from 1206 to 1526. Sultan was a title used by a ruler. Five dynasties ruled in this period. They were Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. Mamluk is also called the Slave dynasty in many books.
A dynasty is a ruling family or line of rulers. Delhi was an important centre, but rulers changed. The area they controlled changed too.
Think of a school that has several heads over time. The school remains, but its leaders and rules may change. This helps explain the sequence. Do not assume every sultan ruled all of India.

s.h: Early rulers and the struggle for power
p: Qutb-ud-din Aibak began independent rule in 1206. Iltutmish strengthened the Sultanate. Razia ruled from 1236 to 1240. Balban later stressed the ruler's power and strict discipline.
A ruler needed support from powerful nobles and army leaders. Nobles were people with high rank and influence. They could help a ruler or challenge the throne.
Razia faced strong opposition, including prejudice against a woman ruler. Her story shows how difficult court politics could be. It does not show that women were unable to govern.
An iqta was a revenue assignment. Revenue means income, often from taxes. An iqta holder collected income from an area and carried out agreed duties. The holder could be called an iqtadar or muqti.
Think of someone given a source of income to pay for a job. The income and the duty are linked. This is a useful comparison for the iqta system.
An iqta was not simply land owned forever by its holder. The ruler tried to keep control and supervise the officials. The details changed from one reign to another.

s.h: Alauddin Khalji: why control market prices?
p: Alauddin Khalji expanded his power and faced Mongol attacks. He needed a large army. Soldiers needed food, horses and other supplies. These all cost money.
He is known for market rules and price controls. He also used checks on soldiers and horses. His commanders led campaigns in the Deccan.

Imagine feeding a large team each day. If food prices rise sharply, the cost grows too. This helps explain why prices mattered to the army. Controls still needed staff and enforcement. They also affected traders and farmers.

s.h: Muhammad bin Tughlaq: bold plans and hard problems
p: Muhammad bin Tughlaq tried token currency. A token coin has a stated value greater than the value of its metal. The plan faced problems, including fake coins and a lack of trust.
Think of a shop voucher. It works only if shops accept it and fake copies are checked. This helps explain the problem. A bold idea can fail when the steps needed to make it work are weak.

He also tried to move the capital towards Daulatabad. Moving a centre of rule over a great distance was hard. People needed transport, homes and ways to keep in touch. His rule also included tax measures in the Doab.

s.h: Later rulers and the end of the Sultanate
p: Firoz Shah Tughlaq is known for canals and other public works. A canal carries water. Later, Delhi's control weakened and regional states grew stronger. Timur invaded Delhi in 1398.
The Sayyids and then the Lodis ruled after the Tughlaqs. The Lodis were of Afghan origin. In 1526, Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat.
That battle marks the usual end of the Sultanate period. It also marks the start of Mughal rule. Do not mix it with the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556.

We learn from coins, buildings, inscriptions and written accounts. Many writers worked near the court. Their views may favour a ruler or reflect elite concerns. So historians compare their claims with other evidence.
Learn the order: Mamluk → Khalji → Tughlaq → Sayyid → Lodi. Then link one idea with each key ruler. Alauddin: market controls. Muhammad bin Tughlaq: token currency. Firoz Shah: canals.
Try this: why was an iqta useful? It linked income with duties. But the ruler also had to stop officials becoming too independent. Understanding the link is better than learning the word alone.

sum: The Sultanate lasted from 1206 to 1526.
Five dynasties ruled in sequence.
Iqta linked revenue with duties; it was not permanent private ownership.
Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.

Mughal Empire.sub: Understand Mughal rulers, ranks, taxes and buildings with easy examples.

p: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in 1526. This was the First Battle of Panipat. It marked the start of Mughal rule. Humayun followed Babur. He lost power to the Sur rulers for a time, then recovered Delhi.
Akbar became ruler in 1556. Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb followed him. Learn the order: Babur → Humayun → Akbar → Jahangir → Shah Jahan → Aurangzeb.
A dynasty is a line of rulers. The Mughal dynasty did not end when Aurangzeb died. Later emperors remained, though their power grew weaker.
Akbar grew the empire through war and alliances. An alliance is an agreement to work together. Many Rajput rulers joined Mughal service. Others resisted. Akbar recruited people from several groups.
Sulh-i kul is often explained as universal peace. It was an important idea in Akbar's rule. It supported an approach of respect across different faiths.

Think of a large team with people from many backgrounds. Cooperation can help the team work well. This helps explain the value of alliances. But it does not mean every ruler joined willingly or all conflict ended.

Mansab means rank or position. A mansabdar held a rank in Mughal service. Two key terms were zat and sawar. Zat related to personal rank and status. Sawar related to the cavalry a mansabdar had to maintain. Cavalry means troops on horses.
Imagine a manager's job grade and the size of the team they lead. These are two different measures. This is a useful comparison for zat and sawar.
Exam tip: personal rank points to zat. Horsemen and cavalry duties point to sawar. Do not swap the two terms.

s.h: Jagir and taxes: where did income come from?
p: Many mansabdars received income through jagirs. A jagir was a revenue assignment. Revenue means income, often from taxes. It gave a right to collect income from an area. It did not automatically give permanent ownership of its land.

Taxes on farming were central to the empire's income. Zamindars were local figures who played varied roles between farmers and the state. Todar Mal is linked with Akbar's revenue system, including zabt.

Zabt used careful records of land, crops and prices where this was possible. Think of estimating a farm's output before setting a tax. A bad harvest could still make payment hard. So tax rules affected real lives, not just accounts.

s.h: Art, buildings and the people who made them
p: Jahangir's reign is known for court painting. Nur Jahan also held great influence. Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal at Agra and the Red Fort in Delhi.
Commissioned means ordered and paid for a work to be made. A ruler's name may be linked with a building. But many artists, builders and workers made it possible.
Imagine a large house being built. It needs plans, materials and skilled people. Royal buildings needed these too, on a much larger scale. Do not give one ruler credit for every Mughal monument.

s.h: Aurangzeb and the strain of a large empire
p: Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 to 1707. The empire covered a very wide area. Long wars in the Deccan used large amounts of money and effort. Conflict and talks with the Marathas and other powers shaped his rule.
Religious policies, tax pressures and rivalries also affected politics. There was no single cause for all the empire's later problems.
Think of a shop adding many branches. More branches may bring more income. They also cost more to manage. In the same way, a larger empire can have more resources and more burdens at once.

After 1707, fights over the throne and stronger regional powers weakened Mughal control. This was a gradual change. Bahadur Shah Zafar was removed after the revolt of 1857. The dynasty formally ended then.
Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama. Its third volume is the Ain-i Akbari. Such court works are valuable, but their claims need to be read with care.
Quick check: mansab is rank. Zat is personal rank. Sawar concerns cavalry duties. Jagir is a revenue assignment. First Panipat was in 1526; Second Panipat was in 1556. Keep these pairs clear.

sum: Babur began Mughal rule in 1526.
Akbar used campaigns, alliances and a broad system of service.
Zat and sawar measured different responsibilities.
Jagirs assigned revenue, not automatically permanent land ownership.
The dynasty ended in 1857, after a long decline in power.

Revolt of 1857.sub: Learn the causes, leaders and results of the revolt step by step.

p: The revolt of 1857 was a major uprising against East India Company rule. Many sepoys took part. A sepoy was an Indian soldier in the Company's army. Rulers, farmers and other groups also joined in several places.
The uprising spread across parts of northern and central India. Not every region joined. The aims of the rebels differed too.

Think of a protest where people have different concerns. Some want better pay. Others want land or political power restored. They may oppose the same ruler without sharing every goal. This helps explain the revolt's range.

s.h: Deeper causes: why were people angry?
p: The Company took over several kingdoms. This process is called annexation. Under the Doctrine of Lapse, it refused to recognise adopted heirs in some states. This policy is linked with Dalhousie.

Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the stated ground of misgovernment. It was not a Doctrine of Lapse case. Tax demands and changes in land control also caused anger. Sepoys had concerns about service rules and religious practices.
Imagine an employer changing pay and working rules again and again. Anger can build before a strike begins. In the same way, several long-term problems existed before the revolt broke out.

Sepoys believed the new Enfield rifle cartridges used cow and pig fat. A cartridge holds what is needed to fire a gun. Soldiers had to bite these cartridges. This raised religious concerns among Hindu and Muslim sepoys.
Mangal Pandey's action at Barrackpore came in March 1857. The major outbreak at Meerut began on 10 May 1857. Rebels then moved to Delhi. They appealed to Bahadur Shah Zafar as a symbolic leader.
Think of a spark lighting dry wood. The cartridges were a spark. The deeper grievances were the wood. A trigger starts an event, but it is not always the only cause.
Delhi: Bahadur Shah Zafar. Kanpur: Nana Sahib. Lucknow and Awadh: Begum Hazrat Mahal. Jhansi: Rani Lakshmibai. Bihar: Kunwar Singh. Tantia Tope also played a major military role.
A mental map can help you learn the names. Place each leader beside a town or region. It is easier than remembering a list without links.
Local aims mattered. Jhansi's case involved the question of succession. Succession means who takes power after a ruler. Do not assume each leader commanded every rebel or had exactly the same plan.

s.h: Why did the revolt fail militarily?
p: The rebels faced problems with supplies, plans and communication. Communication means passing messages. Participation was uneven. Some rulers and groups did not support the uprising. The British and their allies retained important military advantages.
Imagine brave teams acting without a shared plan. They may struggle against an opponent with better supplies and coordination. This helps explain part of the problem.
British repression was harsh, and key centres were recaptured. But failure in battle does not mean an event has no impact. The revolt led to major changes in colonial rule.
The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred rule from the Company to the British Crown. Crown means the British monarchy in this context. India did not become independent.
A Secretary of State for India held major responsibilities in Britain. The Governor-General also served as Viceroy. The army was reorganised. British policy towards Indian princes changed too.

Queen Victoria's proclamation stated promises about rule, religion and princes. A proclamation is a public announcement. Promises in a document do not prove that all were fully honoured. Historians also check what happened in practice.

s.h: Keep causes, events and results separate
p: Use three groups when you revise. Causes: annexation, land and tax pressures, army grievances. Events: Meerut, Delhi and regional resistance. Results: Crown rule and changes in the army.
Common traps: Awadh was not annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. The main Meerut outbreak was on 10 May 1857. Crown rule followed in 1858. It did not end colonial rule.
Try this: why is the cartridge dispute called a trigger? It helped set off the revolt. But other problems had been building for years. A good answer includes both.

sum: The cartridge dispute was a trigger, not the only cause.
The main Meerut outbreak began on 10 May 1857.
Leaders and aims varied across regions.
Rule passed to the British Crown in 1858; India was still under colonial rule.

Freedom Struggle.sub: Follow the freedom struggle through key events and everyday examples.

s.h: How did the national movement grow?
p: India's freedom struggle grew over many decades. People used meetings, writing, protests and other forms of action. The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885. Early leaders used petitions and public debate. A petition is a formal request.
Nationalism is a sense of shared political belonging. Newspapers and groups helped connect people across regions. Yet people had different views about the future nation.

Think of neighbours working together on a common problem. They may share a goal while keeping different needs and opinions. The freedom struggle also involved many groups. Independence was not one person's work alone.
Dadabhai Naoroji is linked with the drain theory. It explained how wealth flowed from India to Britain under colonial rule. Colonial rule means control by a foreign power.
The partition of Bengal in 1905 under Curzon led to strong protests. Partition means division. Swadeshi encouraged locally made goods. Boycott meant refusing selected foreign goods or institutions.

Imagine people choosing local cloth and refusing certain imported goods together. Shopping can then become part of a political campaign. But purchases alone did not end British rule. Meetings, education and organised action also mattered.
Gandhi returned to India in 1915. Champaran in 1917 was an important early campaign. Kheda and Ahmedabad followed in 1918. These struggles dealt with real problems of farmers and workers.
Satyagraha joined truth with nonviolent resistance. Nonviolent means without violence. It involved active, disciplined action against injustice. It was not simply staying quiet.

For example, people may peacefully refuse an unjust rule. They explain their demands and accept the consequences. This helps show the method. Many other leaders and groups also took part in the wider struggle, using different methods.

The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed harsh measures, including detention without trial in certain cases. Detention means being held by the authorities. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place in Amritsar on 13 April 1919.
Non-Cooperation began in 1920. People were urged to withdraw from selected colonial institutions. The campaign was linked with the Khilafat movement, though their aims differed.

Gandhi suspended Non-Cooperation after violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922. Think of a campaign built on a promise of nonviolence. Violence creates a serious conflict with that method. Stopping this campaign did not end the whole freedom struggle.

The Lahore Congress of 1929 called for Purna Swaraj, or complete independence. Nationalists observed 26 January 1930 as Independence Day. That is different from today's Republic Day, which marks 1950.
In 1930, Gandhi marched from Sabarmati to Dandi. He challenged the salt law. Salt mattered because ordinary people across many groups used it every day.

Civil disobedience means openly breaking selected laws seen as unjust. Non-Cooperation stresses refusing cooperation with institutions. The methods could overlap, but their meanings differ. Salt made a large political issue easy to connect with daily life.

s.h: 1942 and the many paths of resistance
p: Quit India began in August 1942. It demanded an end to British rule. Major leaders were arrested, and people resisted in different ways across regions.

Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army in another important strand of struggle. Workers, farmers, women, students and many regional groups also made contributions. The war and later political talks shaped events too.

Think of several streams joining a river. Their routes differ, but they can contribute to a wider flow. This helps explain the range of the struggle. It does not mean all groups agreed about tactics or the future.

India became independent on 15 August 1947. Partition created India and Pakistan. It brought terrible violence and forced many people to leave their homes. Freedom and this suffering both belong in the story.
Revise in order: Congress 1885 → Swadeshi 1905 → Gandhi's return 1915 → repression 1919 → Non-Cooperation 1920 → suspension 1922 → Salt March 1930 → Quit India 1942 → independence 1947.

Common trap: independence and becoming a republic are different events. Learn each movement's method as well as its date. For example, link the Salt March with breaking an unjust law, not just the year 1930.

sum: Many people and groups contributed to the freedom struggle.
Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience mean different things.
Salt March: 1930. Quit India: 1942. Independence: 15 August 1947.
Partition brought violence and displacement alongside freedom.

Post-Independence India.sub: Understand how India built its democracy and faced new challenges after 1947.

p: In 1947, India faced urgent problems. Partition had caused violence. Many people had lost their homes. The new state needed to help refugees, bring princely states into the Union and build democratic institutions.
An institution is an organised body with a public role. Courts and elected legislatures are examples. A constitution was also needed to set out rules for government.
Think of opening a school. A name and a building are only a start. It also needs teachers, funds and fair rules. In the same way, independence began a long task of building a functioning country.

Before independence, India included British-run provinces and princely states. Princes ruled these states under British paramountcy. Paramountcy means the overriding authority held by the British. That authority ended in 1947.

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon played major roles in integration. Integration means bringing parts into a larger whole. Negotiations and accession agreements were important. Accession means joining a state or union.

An Instrument of Accession was a legal document. It set out an agreement on specified matters. But not every state's case was the same. Hyderabad, Junagadh and Jammu and Kashmir involved different disputes and events.

s.h: Constitution: two dates to keep clear
p: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949. It came into force on 26 January 1950. That is when India became a republic. A republic does not have a hereditary monarch as its head of state.
B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee. Many members and committees contributed to the Constitution. It set out institutions, rights and principles for rule.

Think of approving new rules in November but starting to use them in January. Approval and the start date differ. This helps explain adoption and commencement. Neither date is the same as independence on 15 August 1947.

s.h: Voting and the first general election
p: India's first general election took place in 1951–1952. Eligible adults could vote without tests of wealth or education. This principle is called universal adult franchise. Franchise here means the right to vote.
The voting age was first 21. It was later reduced to 18 through the Sixty-first Amendment. An amendment is a formal change to the Constitution.

Imagine a vote where only rich people have a say. Many citizens would be left out. Adult franchise gave a much wider group a voice. Democracy also needs rights, fair institutions and public accountability. Elections alone are not the whole story.
Andhra State was formed in 1953 for Telugu-speaking areas. The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 changed boundaries on a large scale. Language was a major factor in this process.

Think of a local office using a language people understand. It may be easier for them to seek help. But boundaries also affect resources and minority groups. So reorganising states involved many concerns.

Federalism means that different levels of government have defined powers. India has Union and state institutions. Their responsibilities are set out in the Constitution. States are not simply separate countries.

The First Five Year Plan began in 1951. It gave much attention to farming and related needs. The Second Plan stressed heavy industry more strongly. A mixed economy uses both public and private sectors. Public means run by the state; private means run by individuals or firms.
The Green Revolution raised foodgrain output, especially in some regions. Improved seeds worked with water, fertilisers and other support. Benefits and costs were uneven.

Imagine planting a high-yielding seed without enough water. The seed alone cannot solve the problem. Farming also needs resources and markets. In 1991, a serious economic crisis led to major policy reforms. These changed rules on trade, investment and business.

India's later history includes wars, social movements and debates about fairness. The Emergency lasted from 1975 to 1977. It severely restricted civil liberties. Civil liberties are freedoms such as speech and personal freedom.
Learn this order: independence 1947 → Constitution adopted 1949 → republic 1950 → first election 1951–1952 → Andhra State 1953 → state reorganisation 1956 → Emergency 1975–1977 → reforms 1991.

Common traps: the original voting age was 21. The Constitution's adoption and start dates differ. Independence brought great change, but poverty and inequality did not vanish. A balanced answer includes both progress and continuing problems.

sum: India faced refugee support, state integration and institution building after 1947.
Constitution adopted: 26 November 1949. In force: 26 January 1950.
First general election: 1951–1952. Major state reorganisation: 1956.
Voting, rights and accountability all matter to democracy.
Development brought gains but also uneven effects.

Prehistoric Period.sub: Learn about early people through tools, food, homes and clues in the ground.

p: Prehistory is the human past before written records are available for a society. It does not mean people had no language or knowledge. Different regions began leaving written records at different times.
We study tools, bones, pottery and remains of homes. These objects can reveal how people lived. They cannot answer every question about a person's thoughts or name.
Imagine finding a cooking pot without a diary. You may learn about meals from traces in the pot. But you cannot simply guess who owned it. This is why evidence matters.
Archaeologists study material remains of the past. They check where an object was found and what lay near it. Layers in the ground help show how a site changed over time.

Radiocarbon dating can estimate the age of suitable organic remains. Organic remains include things from once-living plants and animals. The method has limits. It does not directly date every stone tool.
Think of a tool beside an old hearth. A hearth is a place used for fire. The objects may help explain each other if the layer is undisturbed. If someone moved them later, the link may be less clear.
Palaeolithic means Old Stone Age. People used stone tools and got much of their food by hunting and gathering. Gathering means collecting foods such as fruits, roots and seeds.
Groups often moved to find food and water. They needed detailed knowledge of places and seasons. Moving did not mean they lacked plans or skills.
Imagine a water source drying up. A group may need to move even if it has good tools. This helps explain how the environment shaped daily choices. Tools also differed across times and places.

s.h: Mesolithic: small tools with useful jobs
p: Mesolithic means Middle Stone Age. Many sites from this period contain microliths. These are small stone tools. People could fit them into handles or combine them with other materials.
Think of a small blade used as part of a larger tool. A tiny piece can still do an important job. That helps explain why microliths were useful.
Hunting and gathering remained important. Ways of living varied. Not every small stone piece is a microlith. Experts check its shape, how it was made and where it was found.

Neolithic means New Stone Age. It is broadly linked with farming and animal domestication. Domestication means bringing plants or animals under human care over time. Many communities also used polished stone tools and pottery.
Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan, is a key early farming site. Burzahom in Kashmir is known for pit dwellings. A pit dwelling is a living space dug into the ground.

If people plant crops, they need to stay near fields to tend them. Stored food can help later. But farming also brings hard work and the risk of crop failure. It did not instantly replace hunting everywhere.
Chalcolithic means Copper–Stone Age. People used copper objects alongside stone tools. Many communities farmed, kept animals and made crafts. Copper did not replace every stone tool at once.
Think of a home that uses both old and new tools. Each may still suit a task. The same basic point helps explain why copper and stone could be used together.
Learn the broad sequence: Palaeolithic → Mesolithic → Neolithic → Chalcolithic. But do not treat it as one exact timetable. Changes happened at different times across regions.
Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is known for rock shelters and paintings. The paintings belong to different periods. A single site can contain traces from many times.
Art gives clues to activities and ideas. But we need care when working out what an image means. We cannot assume every painting at a prehistoric site has the same age.

Ask four questions to revise: what did people eat? What tools did they use? Where did they live? What evidence remains? Common traps: prehistory has no single worldwide end date. Farming grew gradually. Copper and stone could be used together.

sum: Prehistory is studied mainly through material remains.
Palaeolithic: stone tools, hunting and gathering.
Mesolithic: microliths in many contexts.
Neolithic: farming and domestication developed at different times.
Chalcolithic: copper and stone used together.
